title: Second reason: after judgment every unrepented sin—even idle words—meets eternal penalty
source_text: LXV. Praeterea peccata quaelibet, utut levia nobis appareant, post diem judicii, in impoenitentibus poena aeterna punientur; juxta illud Christi apud Matthaeum, Dico autem vobis, quoniam omne verbum otiosum quod locuti fuerint homines, reddent ra-tionem de eo in die judicii. Nec enim post diem judicii ullus locus erit poenis tem-poralibus. Si autem peccata quaevis possunt poena aeterna puniri, & de facto punien-tur in impoenitentibus, proculdubio poena tali digna sunt, & aeternam poenam me-rentur; alioqui Deus injuste ageret, peccatum puniens graviori poena quam ipsi de-beatur: cum contra communis sit sententia Theologorum, Deum peccatores punire infra condignum. Omne autem peccatum quod aeterna poena dignum est mortale dici & vocari potest.
pass_a_gloss: Besides, any sins, however light they appear to us, after the day of judgment will be punished in the impenitent with eternal penalty; according to that word of Christ in Matthew, But I say to you, that every idle word which men shall have spoken, they shall render an account of it in the day of judgment. For after the day of judgment there will be no place for temporal penalties. But if any sins can be punished with eternal penalty, and in fact will be punished in the impenitent, without doubt they are worthy of such a penalty and merit eternal punishment; otherwise God would act unjustly, punishing a sin with a heavier penalty than is due to it: whereas on the contrary the common sentence of theologians is that God punishes sinners below desert. But every sin which is worthy of eternal penalty can be called and named mortal.
pass_b_english: Second proof: post-judgment, no temporal penalties remain—so idle words in the impenitent meet everlasting pain.
If God justly forever-punishes them, they deserve it; theologians already say he punishes below desert—so ‘mortal’ fits.

choices.why: Eternal actual punishment entails eternal desert.
